name: HTTP
purpose: carries web pages from a server to a browser — the agreement every page in the address bar arrives under
note: The four letters at the front of an address are this, which is why a browser puts them there when nobody types them

name: HTTPS
purpose: carries the same pages as HTTP, encrypted, so nobody on the way can read along or change anything
note: The padlock in the browser bar is this protocol and nothing else: it says the line is private, never that the site is honest. A fraudulent shop can have a perfectly good padlock

name: MQTT
purpose: carries tiny messages between devices that report something — a thermometer, a light switch, a door contact
note: The one on this list a person never types. It is here because it is what „smart home" is made of underneath, and because it shows a protocol does not have to involve a browser at all

name: SIP
purpose: sets up a call over the internet — who is calling whom, and on which line the voice will travel
note: People say VOIP for this, and VOIP is not a protocol but a purpose — telephoning over the internet. SIP arranges the call, another protocol carries the voice. The habit of reaching for the roomier drawer is worth noticing in oneself

name: SMTP
purpose: carries a mail from the sender's server to the recipient's
note: Nobody meets this directly — mail simply arrives. It is in for the reader who has seen the four letters in a settings dialog and would like them to mean something

name: Ethernet
purpose: carries data along a cable between the machines in one building — the wired half of every network
note: The oldest agreement still in daily use here, from 1973, and the reason an RJ45 socket on a router in 2026 accepts a cable made decades ago

name: WLAN
purpose: carries the same data as Ethernet through the air, so a device needs no cable to reach the router
note: Germans say WLAN, the rest of the world says Wi-Fi, and both mean the same standard — one of the few cases where the German word is the more technical one

name: Bluetooth
purpose: carries sound and small amounts of data a few metres, between two devices that have been introduced to each other once
note: Named after a Danish king who united tribes, and its mark is his initials in runes. The pairing is the point: unlike WLAN it connects two THINGS, not a thing to a network

name: BLE
purpose: carries the same kind of short-range messages as Bluetooth on so little power that a sensor runs for years on one coin cell
note: Also written BT-LE. It shares a name with Bluetooth and is a different radio protocol underneath — which is why a fitness band pairs in a second and holds for a year, while a headset needs charging every few days

name: Zigbee
purpose: carries tiny messages between the lamps, switches and sensors of a house, each one passing the message along for the others
note: Every device is also a relay, so the network grows stronger with each lamp added — the opposite of WLAN, where more devices means more contention

name: Z-Wave
purpose: does what Zigbee does, on a different radio frequency that walls block less
note: The reason a house often has both: they cannot talk to each other, and whichever the first bought lamp used tends to decide the rest

name: Matter
purpose: lets smart-home devices of different makes work together, whichever app or assistant the owner uses
note: The newest one here, and the first that tries to end the problem rather than add to it — agreed by Apple, Google, Amazon and Samsung together, which had not happened before

name: Thread
purpose: carries the messages Matter sends, over the same kind of self-relaying radio network Zigbee uses
note: Matter and Thread are constantly confused and are two layers of one thing: Thread is the road, Matter is the language spoken on it
